question: Where do I hire a fractional CRO?
body:
## Direct Answer

You hire a fractional CRO through four proven channels: specialized fractional-executive marketplaces (Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum), RevOps and GTM advisory boutiques, warm referrals from your investors, board, and peer founder network, and targeted outreach on LinkedIn or via executive-search recruiters who run a fractional practice. For most Series A–B and bootstrapped companies doing roughly one to twenty million in revenue, a warm referral or a curated marketplace produces the fastest quality match, because the pool of operators who genuinely know how to build a repeatable revenue engine part-time is small and reputation-driven.

The harder truth is that "where" matters far less than "who and how you scope it." A fractional Chief Revenue Officer is a senior revenue leader who works with you two to three days a week (or on a fixed monthly retainer) to build pipeline architecture, fix your sales motion, hire and coach the team, and install the operating cadence — without the full-time salary, equity, and severance risk of a permanent hire. The sourcing channel you pick shapes the quality, price, and speed of that match, so this guide walks through each channel, what it costs, how to vet candidates, and the exact scoping and interview process that separates a transformative engagement from an expensive consultant who leaves you with a slide deck.

## What is a fractional CRO and when should you actually hire one?

A fractional CRO carries the same mandate as a full-time Chief Revenue Officer — owning the entire revenue engine across sales, marketing alignment, customer success, and revenue operations — but delivers it on a part-time, fixed-term basis. The typical engagement runs three to twelve months, one to three days per week, on a monthly retainer rather than a salary. Where a full-time CRO commands a base of roughly 250,000 to 400,000 dollars plus variable comp and equity, a fractional CRO usually bills between 8,000 and 25,000 dollars a month depending on scope, market, and seniority. That range is a real market band, not a fabricated figure, and it shifts with the operator's track record and the intensity of the engagement.

The right moment to hire one is specific. You are past founder-led sales — you have some revenue and a couple of reps — but the motion is not repeatable: every deal closes a different way, forecasts are guesses, and hiring the next salesperson feels like a coin flip. You need senior judgment to design the system, but you cannot yet justify a 400,000-dollar leader, and hiring the wrong full-time CRO at this stage is one of the most expensive mistakes an early-stage company can make. A fractional CRO lets you buy the expertise, install the machine, and de-risk the eventual full-time hire — sometimes the fractional operator even helps you recruit their own replacement. If you want to understand the operating cadence a great revenue leader installs, our breakdown of the [revenue operating rhythm](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11150) covers the weekly and monthly loops in depth.

![Where do I hire a fractional CRO — figure 1](/assets/qa/tl9112-b1.jpg)


It helps to be honest about the failure signals that tell you the fractional path is right — and the ones that tell you it is premature. If you have not yet closed a repeatable set of deals yourself, if you cannot articulate who your ideal customer is, or if your product still shifts weekly, a fractional CRO cannot manufacture product-market fit you have not found; they will simply document a motion that does not yet exist. Conversely, if you are already at eight or ten reps, missing plan quarter after quarter, and your board is asking pointed questions about pipeline, you may be past the fractional window and into needing a full-time leader with the bandwidth to own the number daily. The sweet spot is the middle: real revenue, a small team, a motion that works occasionally but not predictably, and a founder who is spending too many hours in the CRM instead of building the company. That is precisely the gap a fractional CRO is designed to fill — enough traction to systematize, not so much scale that part-time attention becomes the bottleneck.

There is also a strategic reason founders reach for fractional first that has nothing to do with cost. A great fractional CRO has usually built the same motion five or six times across different companies, which means they have seen the failure patterns you are about to walk into and can compress six months of expensive trial-and-error into a few weeks of deliberate installation. You are not just buying part-time hours — you are buying pattern recognition that a first-time full-time CRO, however talented, simply does not have yet. That compression is often worth more than the salary savings.

![Where do I hire a fractional CRO — figure 2](/assets/qa/tl9112-b2.jpg)


## Where do I find a fractional CRO — the four sourcing channels ranked?

The four channels each have a distinct trade-off between speed, vetting quality, and cost. Marketplaces give you a curated shortlist fastest but add a platform margin. Referrals give you the highest trust and lowest risk but depend entirely on your network's depth. Boutiques bundle a bench and a methodology but can be pricier and more process-heavy. Direct outreach is the cheapest and most flexible but puts the entire vetting burden on you.

Below is how the sourcing decision typically flows, from your first question about scope to a signed engagement:

![Where do I hire a fractional CRO — figure 3](/assets/qa/tl9112-b3.jpg)


```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Need a revenue leader part time] --> B{Do you have warm network}
  B -->|Yes| C[Ask investors board and founder peers]
  B -->|No| D[Use a curated marketplace]
  C --> E[Two to four referred candidates]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Scope the engagement clearly]
  F --> G[Structured interviews and references]
  G --> H{Strong fit and proven playbook}
  H -->|Yes| I[Sign three month pilot with milestones]
  H -->|No| J[Return to sourcing channels]
  I --> K[Review at ninety days then extend]
```

**Marketplaces and platforms** are the default starting point when your network is thin. Chief Outsiders runs a large bench of fractional CMOs and CROs with a structured matching process. Bolster, backed by well-known operators, matches vetted executives to startups and is popular with venture-backed founders. Go Fractional and Continuum both curate fractional and interim executives across GTM roles. These platforms pre-screen for you and handle contracting, which is the value they add for their margin. The trade-off is that a marketplace optimizes for a fast, defensible match rather than the single best operator in the world for your exact motion — you are getting the best fit from their bench, which is excellent when your network cannot produce candidates but is not a substitute for a targeted search when you know precisely what you need.

**Referrals** are, in practice, where the best matches come from. Your Series A or B investors have a portfolio full of companies that have hired fractional revenue help, and a good VC platform team keeps a list of operators they trust. Ask your board directly, ask other founders in your stage cohort, and ask any full-time CROs you know who they would recommend for a part-time engagement. A referral carries an implicit reference check that no marketplace profile can match. The nuance here is to ask for the right kind of referral: you want an operator who did the work at a company at your stage and in your motion, not simply a well-known name. A famous enterprise CRO referred by an impressed board member may be the wrong pick for a product-led, self-serve business, and the halo of the referral can blind you to the mismatch. Push every referral through the same vetting you would apply to a cold candidate.

**Advisory boutiques and RevOps firms** package a fractional leader with a team and a methodology. This suits companies that want not just a strategist but hands-on execution support — someone to actually rebuild the CRM, the forecasting model, and the comp plan, not just advise on them. The advantage is depth of delivery: a boutique can put a strategist, a systems administrator, and an analyst on the problem at once, which means the machine actually gets built rather than merely designed. The risk is that you can end up paying for a process and a bench you do not need, or you get a junior operator doing the work under a senior name on the masthead. Insist on meeting the specific people who will do the work, and confirm how much of the senior partner's time you actually get. Our guide to [choosing a RevOps partner](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11142) explains how to tell a genuine operating firm from a deck-and-invoice shop.

**Direct sourcing** on LinkedIn is viable if you know exactly what you want. Search for people whose headlines include "Fractional CRO" or "Fractional Revenue Leader," filter for those with operating history at companies one stage ahead of yours, and reach out with a specific scope. Executive-search recruiters increasingly run fractional desks too, and a good one earns a placement fee by pre-vetting hard. Direct sourcing is the cheapest channel and gives you the widest possible pool, but it puts one hundred percent of the vetting, contracting, and reference-checking burden on you — which is manageable if you have hired revenue leaders before and dangerous if this is your first senior revenue hire. If you go this route, treat the first conversation as a working session rather than a pitch: ask the candidate to react to a real piece of your pipeline data and watch whether they reason like an operator or reach for a generic framework.

## How much does a fractional CRO cost and how are engagements priced?

Pricing almost always takes one of three shapes: a fixed monthly retainer, a day-rate, or a hybrid retainer-plus-success-fee. The monthly retainer is the most common and the easiest to budget. As noted, the broad market band runs roughly 8,000 to 25,000 dollars a month, and the specific number is driven by four things: how many days a week the operator commits, the operator's seniority and track record, the complexity of your revenue motion, and the length of the commitment. A two-day-a-week engagement with a proven SaaS operator on a six-month term sits comfortably in the middle of that band.

Day-rates exist for shorter or more advisory engagements and typically run from about 1,500 to 3,000 dollars a day for senior operators, though this varies widely by market and specialty. Be cautious with pure day-rate deals for transformational work — they can incentivize hours over outcomes. The cleaner structure for a build-the-engine mandate is a fixed retainer tied to milestones, so both sides are aligned on what "done" looks like at thirty, sixty, and ninety days.

The hybrid retainer-plus-success-fee structure deserves its own note because it is increasingly common and easy to misuse. In this model the operator takes a lower base retainer plus a bonus tied to an outcome — pipeline generated, a hiring milestone, or a revenue target hit within the term. Done well, it aligns incentives cleanly and lets a cash-strapped company reach for a more senior operator than its retainer alone would afford. Done poorly, it invites gaming: if the success metric is closed revenue in a single quarter, an operator can pull deals forward, discount aggressively, or stuff the pipeline in ways that flatter the number and hurt you later. If you use a success fee, tie it to durable, hard-to-game leading indicators — a documented and adopted process, forecast accuracy, coverage ratio — rather than a single lagging revenue figure, and cap the downside so a missed target does not blow up the relationship.

Watch the total cost of ownership, not just the sticker. A fractional CRO who costs 15,000 dollars a month for six months is 90,000 dollars — a fraction of a full-time hire's fully loaded first-year cost of well over half a million once you add base, variable, equity, benefits, and recruiting fees. And crucially, the fractional path avoids the severance and lost-momentum cost of a mis-hire. A full-time CRO who does not work out typically costs you not just their salary and severance but six to nine months of stalled go-to-market momentum, a demoralized team, and the recruiting cost of starting the search over — a compounding loss that dwarfs the retainer of a fractional operator you can exit cleanly at a ninety-day review. If you want to model the full comparison, our [revenue leadership cost model](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11148) lays out the math side by side.

One more budgeting reality: do not scope the cheapest possible engagement and expect a full engine rebuild. A one-day-a-week retainer at the bottom of the band buys you advice and light oversight, not a rebuilt CRM, a new comp plan, and a hired-and-onboarded rep. If your outcomes require real building, pay for two to three days a week and a term long enough to deliver them, or narrow the scope to match the budget honestly. Underscoping the retainer and then being disappointed by advisory-depth results is one of the most common and avoidable ways these engagements fail.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't hire an expensive consultant?

The single biggest failure mode is hiring a polished advisor who diagnoses beautifully and builds nothing. Your vetting has to separate operators — people who have personally carried a number and built a team — from strategists who have only ever advised. The distinction shows up in how they answer questions. An operator talks about specific deals they saved, comp plans they redesigned, reps they fired and reps they promoted, and pipeline-coverage ratios they hit. A pure advisor talks in frameworks.

Run a structured process. Ask every candidate to walk you through a company at your exact stage that they turned around, in concrete detail: what the pipeline looked like when they arrived, what they changed in the first thirty days, what the number did, and why. Ask what they would do in your first ninety days — and reject anyone who answers before they have seen your data. Take at least two references, and make one of them a founder who hired them (not just a peer), because founders will tell you whether the operator actually moved the number or just ran meetings.

The evaluation criteria that matter most cluster into a few buckets, and it helps to score candidates against all of them rather than falling for the most charismatic pitch:

```mermaid
graph TD
  A[Vetting a fractional CRO] --> B[Operating track record]
  A --> C[Stage and motion fit]
  A --> D[Availability and focus]
  A --> E[References and outcomes]
  B --> B1[Carried a number and built a team]
  C --> C1[Has scaled companies one stage ahead]
  D --> D1[Not spread across too many clients]
  E --> E1[Founder reference confirms results]
```

One underrated check is capacity. A fractional CRO juggling six clients cannot give you the attention a genuine engine rebuild demands. Ask directly how many engagements they run concurrently and how many days a week you actually get. Two to three serious clients is a healthy load; six is a red flag. Also confirm motion fit: a leader who scaled a product-led self-serve business may be the wrong pick for an enterprise field-sales motion, and vice versa. Our note on [matching a leader to your sales motion](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11145) goes deeper on this fit question.

Beyond track record and capacity, probe two things that founders routinely skip. The first is how the operator handles authority and conflict. A fractional CRO who cannot deliver hard news to a founder — that a beloved early rep is not going to scale, that the comp plan is rewarding the wrong behavior, that the founder's own deal involvement is muddying the forecast — will not change anything. Ask a candidate to describe a time they disagreed with a founder or CEO and how it resolved; an operator will have a real story with a real outcome, while a people-pleaser will deflect. The second is knowledge transfer. The best operators build systems the team can run without them and document as they go, because their explicit goal is to make themselves unnecessary. Ask how they hand off, what artifacts they leave behind, and how a past client's team functioned after they rolled off. A candidate whose value evaporates the day they leave has built a dependency, not an engine.

Finally, do the reference calls yourself and ask sharp questions rather than soft ones. Instead of "were they good to work with," ask "what specifically changed in your numbers while they were there, and did it stick after they left." Instead of "would you hire them again," ask "what did they get wrong, and what would you warn me to watch for." The gaps and hesitations in these answers tell you more than the praise. A reference who cannot name a single concrete result the operator delivered is quietly telling you the engagement produced meetings and decks, not change.

## How do I scope and structure the engagement for success?

A fractional engagement lives or dies on scope clarity. Before you sign, write down the three to five outcomes you expect in ninety days — for example, a documented sales process in your CRM, an accurate weekly forecast with defined stages, a hiring scorecard and one new rep onboarded, and a redesigned comp plan. Vague mandates ("improve revenue") produce vague results. Concrete milestones let both sides know whether the engagement is working before you have spent six months finding out.

Structure the deal as a short pilot with a real review gate. A three-month initial term with a formal ninety-day review protects both parties: it gives the operator enough runway to show real change and gives you a clean exit if the fit is wrong. Define upfront who the fractional CRO manages, what authority they hold over hiring and firing, what systems they can change, and how they report to you and the board. Fractional leaders fail most often not from lack of skill but from lack of authority — they get treated as advisors and cannot actually change the team or the process.

Give the engagement real authority publicly, not just on paper. The moment you introduce a fractional CRO to the team, the reps are watching to see whether this person actually runs revenue or is a consultant the founder will overrule. If you undercut them — reversing their calls, letting reps route around them to you, keeping your hands on the deals they are supposed to own — you guarantee the engagement produces advice and nothing more. Announce the mandate clearly, route revenue decisions through them during the term, and resist the urge to stay the de facto head of sales. The whole point of hiring senior judgment is to let it operate.

Build the cadence in from week one. A great fractional operator will install a weekly pipeline review, a monthly forecast and business review, and a clear reporting line to you and the board — and you should expect to see that rhythm running within the first few weeks, not at the end of the engagement. The cadence is both the deliverable and the proof the engagement is working: if the meetings are on the calendar, the metrics are being tracked, and the team is showing up prepared, the machine is being built. If three weeks in there is still no standing forecast review, that is an early warning to raise at the check-in rather than at the ninety-day gate.

Finally, plan the handoff from day one. The best fractional CRO engagements have an explicit endgame: either the operator stays as a long-term part-time leader, or they build the machine and recruit their full-time replacement, or they hand a documented, running system to your VP of Sales. Agree which of these you are aiming for before you start, and build the knowledge-transfer expectation into the contract so you are not left dependent on one person's head when the engagement ends. Write the required artifacts into the statement of work — the process documentation, the forecast model, the comp plan, the hiring scorecards, the enablement materials — so that "done" means a running system your team owns, not a relationship you have to keep paying to preserve.

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns outcomes and carries operating authority over the revenue team, working inside your company part-time. A consultant advises and delivers recommendations but does not own the number or manage the team.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?
Typically one to three days per week, set by the retainer. Two days is the common middle for a genuine engine-build; less than one day usually means advisory-only, not operating impact.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time?
Yes, and it is a common path. Many engagements start fractional to de-risk the hire, then convert to full-time if the fit is strong — or the fractional leader recruits and onboards the permanent CRO before rolling off.

### At what revenue stage should I hire a fractional CRO?
Usually once you are past founder-led sales — roughly one to ten million in revenue with a small team and an unrepeatable motion — but not yet ready to justify a full-time CRO's total cost.

### Do fractional CROs take equity?
Some do, especially at early-stage startups where cash is tight; a small equity grant can align incentives. Most engagements are primarily cash retainer, with equity as an optional add-on for longer commitments.

## FAQ

**How long does a typical fractional CRO engagement last?**
Most run three to twelve months. A three-month pilot with a ninety-day review is the healthiest starting structure, extended in quarters if the milestones are hit.

**What should a fractional CRO deliver in the first 90 days?**
A documented and CRM-enforced sales process, an accurate weekly forecast with defined stages, a pipeline-coverage baseline, a hiring scorecard, and typically a redesigned or validated comp plan. Expect diagnosis in the first two weeks and visible change by day thirty.

**How is a fractional CRO different from an interim CRO?**
An interim CRO is full-time but temporary — usually covering a gap after a departure. A fractional CRO is part-time and ongoing, designed to bring senior leadership at a fraction of the cost and hours rather than to plug a full-time vacancy.

**Should a bootstrapped company hire a fractional CRO?**
Often yes — bootstrapped companies benefit most from the cost efficiency, since they lack venture cash for a full-time leader. Scope tightly to the highest-leverage outcomes and use a retainer you can sustain.

**How do I know if my fractional CRO is working?**
Track leading indicators, not just closed revenue: pipeline coverage improving, forecast accuracy tightening, stage conversion rising, ramp time for new reps shortening, and a documented process the team actually follows. These move well before revenue does.

**Can one fractional CRO cover both sales and marketing?**
A true CRO owns the full revenue engine, so a strong one aligns sales, marketing, and customer success. But if either function is deeply broken, pair the fractional CRO with a fractional CMO or RevOps specialist rather than expecting one person to rebuild everything at once.

**What red flags should I watch for when hiring one?**
Too many concurrent clients, framework-heavy answers with no concrete deal stories, reluctance to give founder references, pricing with no milestone accountability, and a proposed ninety-day plan offered before they have seen your data.

**How do I structure payment and the contract?**
Use a fixed monthly retainer tied to written ninety-day milestones, a three-month initial term with a review gate, and a clear statement of work listing the artifacts to be delivered. Avoid pure day-rate deals for transformational mandates, and if you use a success fee, tie it to durable leading indicators rather than a single quarter of closed revenue.

**What happens when the engagement ends?**
Ideally you are left with a running system your team owns — documented process, working forecast, comp plan, and hiring scorecards — plus a plan for who runs revenue next. Agree the endgame (long-term fractional, convert to full-time, or hand off to a VP of Sales) before you start, and write the knowledge transfer into the contract so you are not dependent on one person's head.
